newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mandela woos Buthelezi with high office.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mandela woos Buthelezi with high office.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela is wooing his main black rival Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi by offering him a seat in a ruling triumvirate, government and party sources said on Monday.
"There are a number of options for Mr Buthelezi, but the main one on offer is to make him a deputy president alongside Deputy President (Thabo) Mbeki," a senior government source told Reuters.

A source in the ruling African National Congress (ANC) said Buthelezi, currently a minister in Mandela's cabinet, was interested in the proposal, but he had not yet set terms or met Mandela for formal talks on the idea.
The offer is the latest move in political realignments ahead of South Africa's second democratic elections in 1999.

Former president F.W. de Klerk gave up a position as deputy president alongside Mbeki when he pulled his National Party out of the unity government last year and now his white-led party is seeking allies, possibly including Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), to fight the dominance of the ANC.

Other changes to the political landscape include the possibility of a new party being formed by former NP strategist Roelf Meyer and expelled ANC dissident Bantu Holomisa, who has significant support among disaffected ANC members.
Democratic Party leader Tony Leon, who has also been in talks with the Inkatha leader, said there were signs that a shake-up in South African politics was imminent.
"It's starting to happen and I think it is to be welcomed. I think the old divisions will give way to new and hopefully more realistic ones," he said.

Leon described Mandela's offer to Buthelezi as a "political bauble", but conceded that the ANC would have more than any other party to offer the Zulu leader as parties reassess their alliances ahead of the 1999 polls.

Mandela will not be standing in those elections. He plans to give up the party presidency this year and retire when his current term ends. Mbeki is heir-apparent and effectively prime minister to him at present.
The ANC source said Mandela was anxious in the short term to end the bloody turf war between his ANC and Buthelezi's IFP in KwaZulu-Natal, the country's most populous province.
"The idea is to make peace work in KwaZulu-Natal and ultimately perhaps to unify the two parties into one," he said.
Conflict between the ANC and the IFP has claimed more than 20,000 lives in the past decade.
Jacob Zuma, the ANC's provincial leader in KwaZulu-Natal, said on Sunday that six months of peace talks had produced a firm proposal which was currently being considered by the IFP.

He said the package, which included proposals for a special amnesty process, could see Buthelezi promoted from his current post -- minister of home affairs in a transitional coalition scheduled to end in 1999 -- to a longer-term position.
